I have auto-formalized some solutions to Erdős problems. I was looking into which solutions to Erdős problems might be the hardest to formalize unconditionally, and I think there's one whose solution currently goes via (the solution to) the Weil conjectures. (Another solution needs it for curves only.)

For now, it may be worthwhile to formalize the conditional implication. Accordingly, I am curious: is there a Lean statement of the Weil conjectures available anywhere?
#Model comparisons for Lean > LeanEval @ 💬
I think @Christian Merten had formalized the statement recently
Thank you, @Rado Kirov, for pointing me to @Junyan Xu's PR!

Thank you @Adam Topaz for mentioning @Christian Merten.

I think the statement is available here:
https://github.com/chrisflav/proetale/blob/zeta-function/Proetale/WeilConjectures/Statement.lean

Note:

Weil's fourth conjecture — if X lifts to a smooth proper scheme over a number ring, then deg Pᵢ is the i-th Betti number of the associated complex manifold — needs singular cohomology of the analytification and is not stated here.
Yes, that's the statement I had in mind. Christian told me (in person) that he had the statement written down about two weeks ago :)
And yeah, to state the fourth conjecture we would indeed need both singular cohomology (embarrassingly still not in mathlib as far as I know) and the analytification functor.
@Boris Alexeev do you need the cohomological statement for the Erdos problem?
(My understanding is the lean-eval version also doesn't have this.)
I honestly have no idea, but I assume not!

Boris Alexeev said:

(My understanding is the lean-eval version also doesn't have this.)

Yes, that's right (at least based on the link mentioned above. i.e. https://github.com/leanprover/lean-eval/pull/500 ).
The relevant problem is https://www.erdosproblems.com/157 which mentions a proof by Pilatte, which itself uses a result of Sawin, which is downstream of Weil.
Presumably at this moment, the easiest method of unconditionally formalizing a solution to this problem is to ask AI to think of a different solution. :)
An extremely fast read suggests just the Riemann hypothesis is needed.

FWIW, we probably could state the cohomological assertion. We don't need much from the theory of singular cohomology (for the statement) except that you can compute dimensions of the cohomology groups, and we can patch together a definition of singular (co)homology along the lines of this. We then just need to construct the analytification just as a topological space, which shouldn't be too hard.
I remember having some discussions with @Kevin Buzzard a long time ago about constructing the strong topology on the C\mathbb{C}C-points...
Here is the relevant thread for the strong topology: #maths > top space / manifold structure on points of alg varieties
I thought @Andrew Yang did something towards that?

I only PRed the affine case so the topology itself is never in mathlib but it should be 

import Mathlib

open CategoryTheory

namespace AlgebraicGeometry

open scoped CommRingCat.HomTopology
noncomputable
instance {R : Type*} [CommRing R] [IsLocalRing R] [TopologicalSpace R]
    [IsOpenUnits R] {X : Scheme} : TopologicalSpace (Spec (.of R) ⟶ X) :=
  ⨆ U : X.affineOpens, .coinduced (Spec.map · ≫ U.2.fromSpec) inferInstance

end AlgebraicGeometry

Boris Alexeev said:

An extremely fast read suggests just the Riemann hypothesis is needed.

I understand you meant RH for curves, but still funny. If I recall, isn't the best bound on small gaps between primes relying on Weil?

RH for curves is easy and known to Weil, probably formalizable by current AI within hours (if not yet done). Sawin's paper relies on the full strength of RH for high-dimensional varieties over finite fields and even beyond that (his varieties are not smooth and he needs perverse sheaves and to bound dimension of the cohomology groups). The references I gave for Weil conjectures don't cover perverse sheaves, but they're dealt with in another book Weil Conjectures, Perverse Sheaves and ℓ-adic Fourier Transform, but even this book doesn't seem to cover Saito's work on characteristic cycles used in this prerequisite paper of Sawin.

Zhang's original paper (bound subsequently improved to 4680 in https://arxiv.org/abs/1402.0811) depends on Deligne's work on RH to prove some bounds on exponential sums to establish Motohashi-Pintz-Zhang estimates between the Bombieri-Vinogradov theorem and the Elliott-Halberstam conjecture. Maynard developed a more flexible “multidimensional” version of the Selberg sieve, which is used to establish the better bound 246 (as in LeanEval) in https://arxiv.org/abs/1407.4897 without using any equidistribution results on primes beyond the BV theorem, in particular not relying on Deligne's work.

Junyan Xu said:

RH for curves is easy and known to Weil, probably formalizable by current AI within hours (if not yet done).

I believe it’s already been done here: https://github.com/math-inc/RiemannHypothesisCurves

They use the Bombieri-Stepanov polynomial method to prove a 5mq1/25mq^{1/2}5mq1/2 bound only for hyperelliptic curves, while the optimal is like mq1/2mq^{1/2}mq1/2 (mmm is about twice the genus, which is the dimension of the middle cohomology). The appendix of Michael Rosen, Number Theory in Function Fields is a 11-page proof of RH in full generality, which uses Riemann-Roch (recently formalized):


Stichtenoth also presents essentially the same proof in 10 pages as 5.2 The Hasse-Weil Theorem.
